newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Pakistan says world should talk to the Taleban.
newsitem.headline: Pakistan says world should talk to the Taleban.

text.p: Pakistan on Tuesday said it was time the U.N. Security Council talked to the Taleban movement, which it said had the support of the Afghan people.

While numerous council members during a public debate on Afghanistan criticised the Taleban's treatment of women, Pakistan's ambassador, Ahmad Kamal, said the 18-year old civil war could not be solved without them.

"We have not heard from the true voice of the Afghan people, who alone can decide on their own future," he said. "It is high time that the Security Council should listen to the views of the Taleban in order to have a more balanced view of the situation in Afghanistan."

He said the Taleban has proclaimed it did not want to rule Aghanistan alone and would include other groups in a government. But in the meantime it controlled two-thirds of the country "and cannot simply be wished away," he said.

"Given the support that they undoubtedly have from the population in all the provinces that they control, it would be futile to indulge in name-calling or wishful thinking or in military confrontation," Kamal said. "It would be far better obviously to engage them in constructive dialogue in an effort to get them to moderate some of their policies."

The council is currently discussing Afghanistan, although there are few new ideas to bring the warring factions together. All members agree on negotiations between the combatants, including the Taleban, are necessary in the country's ongoing civil war.
But the Taleban has been singled out by most members for its treatment of women, banned from the workplace and schools, forced to wear veils over their faces and punished severely if they disobey.

Afghanistan's U.N. seat, which the Taleban would like to occupy, is still taken by the government of Burhanuddin Rabbani. Kamal said the seat should be left vacant, noting that Pakistan recognised whatever regime controlled Kabul.
He said the Rabbani government, rather than organising elections, had held onto power with little backing from the population, thereby leading to the current situation.

In response, A.R. Ghafoorzai, the acting foreign minister of the ousted Rabbani government, said his group never advocated the Taleban be excluded from shaping the future of Afghanistan but that the movement had rejected proposals for negotiations.
He accused Kamal of giving legitimacy to mercenaries who are "trained, financed armed and equipped in Pakistani territory."
Pakistan, as well as Saudi Arabia, deny accusations of arming the Taleban. Russia and Iran support opposition factions and are also accused of arming them.
